name: Bilal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for giving me your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollins Mutual, an old insurer in the market town where I grew up. It's owned by its members, not shareholders, and the office still has the founder's portrait on the stairs. I do claims for vans and farm vehicles: a tractor in a ditch, a builder's van with the tools nicked. I take the details on the phone, fill in the claim, chase the garage for the repair quote and file it all for the senior to sign off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people know us. Half the farmers who ring knew my granddad. The hard bit is the computer side; I'm slow on the system and I write everything on paper first, then type it up, which Mr Ashworth, my manager, says doubles my time. He's patient, but he's mentioned it twice now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never thought it was as clever as they made out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work and down at the club: told you so, a computer can't talk to a farmer. I'm not online much, except the church group chat, and I'd keep it off there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I've still got worries. I'm getting married next June and the wedding's costing more than we planned. And Hollins is small; the big insurers undercut us every year, and Mr Ashworth hasn't replaced two people who left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to stop writing everything on paper first, since that's what slows me. I'd keep saving for the wedding and the house deposit, we've got about three months' worth put by. I wouldn't change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, but uneasy about Hollins itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight with the wedding, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the reception. Hana and I would do it at the church hall instead of the hotel, if we had to. My mum would be cross, but she'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy about Hollins, if AI isn't the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the two empty desks, really. Nobody says Hollins is in trouble, but nobody's hired either. If a bigger firm bought Hollins, I don't think they'd keep a slow junior who writes on paper.

say: I'd say **told you so**: a computer can't talk to a farmer.
I'd keep AI off the **church group chat** entirely.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but Hollins is small and being undercut every year.
Two **empty desks** haven't been filled, and nobody says why.
do: Stop **writing on paper** first, since that doubles my time.
Keep saving for **the wedding** and a house deposit.
Move the reception to the **church hall** if money gets tight.
feel: Mostly settled, but **uneasy** about Hollins itself.
S0.quote: If a bigger firm bought Hollins, I don't think they'd keep a slow junior who writes on paper.
fieldNote: His worry is **the firm**, not AI: a small mutual losing ground.
The **wedding** is the household's big cost and focus.
He trusts **personal relationships** with farmers over any technology.

steps.text: Type claims straight into the system instead of on paper
Move the wedding reception to the church hall if needed
Keep adding to the wedding and house deposit savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the big firms' world. Hollins would be the last to go that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the members want a person on the phone, and that's what a mutual is for. I'd say it at the club too. I'd mean it, but I'd be saying it partly to reassure myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd catch up with us. If the big firms do claims with AI and charge less, Hollins either follows or gets bought. Either way, the job I do, taking details and filling in forms, is exactly the stuff on your card, and I'm slowest at the computer part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back now: no new car, a cheaper honeymoon, and keep every bit I can in savings. I wouldn't learn the AI stuff unless Hollins made me. I'd talk to my dad about roofing, he's got his own small firm, just to know the door's open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like when you hear a noise downstairs at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the AI tools unless made to. Why not, if it might keep you in a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's how I am. I don't see the point of learning something that's there to replace me. I'd rather put the time into a trade that's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the machines, they're just machines. The people running big companies who want to cut costs, and the government for not caring what happens to towns like ours.

I'd say it at the **club** too, partly to reassure myself.
think: Hollins either **follows or gets bought** if big firms do claims cheaper.
My job is **exactly the stuff** on the card, and I'm slowest at computers.
do: Skip the **new car** and book a cheaper honeymoon.
Ask my dad if his **roofing firm** door is open.
Avoid **learning AI** unless Hollins makes me.
feel: **Worried**, like a noise downstairs at night.
S1.quote: I don't see the point of learning something that's there to replace me. I'd rather put the time into a trade that's real.
fieldNote: He **refuses AI** on principle and turns to his father's trade instead.
He blames **big company owners** and a distant government, not the machines.
His public line about **mutual values** is partly for his own comfort.

steps.text: Skip the new car and book a cheaper honeymoon
Ask his dad whether the roofing firm could take him on
Wait until Hollins requires AI training before learning it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? With a wedding in June? You're joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain and simple, and the people who did it should have to answer for it. I'd vote for whoever said they'd protect jobs and towns, not handouts, real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Hollins either shuts or becomes a computer with a logo. My job goes, and quickly. There's no part of claims that's hands-on, it's all phone and forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad straight away and start roofing with him, labouring at first, learning the trade properly. I'd keep the Hollins job as long as it lasted, evenings and weekends on the roofs. We'd still get married, but small, in the church hall, and the house would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the ground's tipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says hands-on robots come about three years later. What does that mean for the roofing plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my lifeline. If roofs need people for about three years longer than offices, then my dad's trade carries me while I work out the next thing. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd have a skill and my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fiancée say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana teaches at the infant school. She'd say we'll manage, we've got each other and family. She'd be right, but I'd still feel like I let her down before we started.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and those who did it should answer for it.
I'd vote for whoever protects **real work**, not handouts.
think: Hollins **shuts or becomes** a computer with a logo.
Claims has **nothing hands-on**; it's all phone and forms.
do: Start **roofing with my dad**, labouring first, while Hollins lasts.
Hold a **small wedding** in the church hall and delay the house.
Vote for whoever promises to **protect jobs** in towns.
S2.quote: Hollins either shuts or becomes a computer with a logo.
fieldNote: He leans on **family**: his father's trade and his fiancée's steady job.
The **three-year robot gap** makes roofing a lifeline in his mind.
He feels he's **letting down** his fiancée before they've started.

steps.text: Start labouring on roofs with his dad on evenings and weekends
Hold a small church hall wedding and put off buying a house
Vote for candidates promising to protect jobs in towns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: back the people who work, back apprenticeships, keep the money in the town. I'd say Hollins should be helping its own staff move, like a proper mutual would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same answer, just slower. I'd move into roofing, but I'd have time to do it properly, with a real apprenticeship instead of just labouring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, then start a proper roofing apprenticeship through the college in year two, with my dad as my employer. I'd stay at Hollins part-time if Mr Ashworth would let me. I'd keep saving, maybe to five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried still, but I'd have a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel telling your manager you were going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Mr Ashworth gave me my first job. I'd want to tell him face to face and thank him. That's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay if Hollins promised to keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. If Hollins could promise me a desk till the end, I'd probably stay. I'm not someone who jumps. But they couldn't promise that.

say: I'd back **apprenticeships** and keeping money in the town.
I'd say Hollins should help **its own staff** move, like a proper mutual.
think: It's the **same answer** as the fast one, just slower, and my desk still goes.
I'd have time for a **real apprenticeship** through the college, not just labouring.
do: Have **the wedding** as planned next June.
Start a **roofing apprenticeship** through the college in year two.
Ask to stay at Hollins **part-time** while training.
S3.quote: If Hollins could promise me a desk till the end, I'd probably stay. I'm not someone who jumps.
fieldNote: Extra time turns labouring into a **proper apprenticeship**.
**Loyalty** to his manager shapes how he'd leave.
He admits he'd **stay** if he could, which shows his resistance to change.

steps.text: Start a roofing apprenticeship at the college in year two
Ask Mr Ashworth to keep him on part-time while training
Build savings up to five months after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and no need to panic. People said the internet would end everything too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Hollins and hope. I'd probably watch it for a few years before doing anything. But I'd know in the back of my mind that my dad's trade is the backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollins, get married, try for children, and buy a house in town. I'd only learn the computer stuff Hollins made me learn. Around year five I'd look again, and if it was still coming, I'd start roofing then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your family in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want our children in a house we own, with me in a steady job. That's the plan whatever happens. Ten years means I'd probably get the first bit done before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd leave the switch too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, by then. If I waited too long, I'd be thirty-five starting an apprenticeship with lads of sixteen, and my dad might have retired. I know that.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and no need to panic.
People said **the internet** would end everything too.
think: I'd **stay and hope**, watching for a few years first.
My **dad's trade** stays the backup in my mind.
do: Get married, **try for children** and buy a house in town.
Learn only the **compulsory** computer systems at Hollins.
S4.quote: If I waited too long, I'd be thirty-five starting an apprenticeship with lads of sixteen, and my dad might have retired.
fieldNote: With a decade he'd **wait and hope**, true to his resistance.
**Family** comes first: children and a house in town.
He knows the **risk of waiting**: his father retiring and an older start.

steps.text: Try for children and buy a house in town
Wait until about year five before deciding on roofing
Stay at Hollins doing only the compulsory computer training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, with the wedding and everything. What would help is proper apprenticeships for grown men, paid enough to live on, and firms like Hollins putting money into training their own people instead of just letting them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about towns. Hollins is half the reason our high street has a café. If it goes, it's not just my job, it's the sandwich shop and the bus to the office.

headlineQuote: Hollins is half the reason our high street has a café. If it goes, it's not just my job, it's the sandwich shop and the bus to the office.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** van and farm vehicle claims clerk at Hollins Mutual in his home market town.
He's **engaged**, marrying next June, with about three months saved.
He **never uses AI** and writes claims on paper before typing them up.
As things speed up, he turns to his father's **roofing firm** as a hands-on lifeline.
He's **traditional**: he blames big firms and distant government and wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, coming right as he marries.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, and employers training their **own staff**.
